524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

580: ## 8. CONFIGURATION TEMPLATES

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example
721: 
722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete
755: 
756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations
760: - Annotate non-obvious parts
761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout
764: - Follow patterns from other assets in the skill
765: - Match style of SKILL.md
766: - Use consistent formatting
767:

769: 
770: ## 10. ASSET FILE CHECKLIST
771: 
772: **Before creating an asset file, verify**:
773: 
774: ```markdown

794: Integration:
795: □ SKILL.md references this asset where appropriate
796: □ Asset complements (doesn't duplicate) SKILL.md content
797: □ File size appropriate (typically 100-800 lines)
798: □ Content is self-contained (doesn't require external context)
799: ```

855: ## 12. ASSET MAINTENANCE
856: 
857: ### When to Update Assets
858: 
859: **Update asset files when**:
860: - New template variations emerge
861: - User feedback reveals confusion
862: - Standards or conventions change
863: - New use cases discovered
864: - Examples become outdated
865: 
866: **Version control**:
867: - Note significant changes in skill version bump
868: - Keep examples current with latest patterns
869: - Remove deprecated templates
870: - Add migration notes for breaking changes
871: 
872: ### Deprecation Strategy
873: 
874: **If removing a template**:
875: 1. Mark as deprecated in section header: `## DEPRECATED: Template Name`
876: 2. Explain why deprecated and what to use instead
877: 3. Keep for 1-2 skill versions (with deprecation warning)
878: 4. Remove after migration period

881: ```markdown
882: ## DEPRECATED: OLD TEMPLATE NAME
883: 
884: ⚠️ **This template is deprecated as of v3.0.0**
885: 
886: **Use instead**: `new-template-name.md` (see Section 2)

888: **Migration**: Replace X with Y in your existing files
889: ```

14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides

123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227:

274: ```

279: - Description of field

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.

165: description: "[One-sentence description]"

167:   - "[search phrase]"

15: 
16: # create-with-human-voice
17: 
18: > Turn a draft that reads like a machine wrote it into one that does not, and show the numbers that prove the pass happened.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
23: 
24: | Aspect | What you get |
25: |---|---|
26: | **Use it for** | Applying the Human Voice Rules to prose, or scoring prose against them |
27: | **Invoke with** | `@markdown /create:with-human-voice`, which the command requires and hard-blocks without, or "make this sound human", or a direct read of `SKILL.md` |
28: | **Works on** | A file, a passage, a reply, or a draft you are part way through |
29: | **Produces** | An edited target plus a before and after report, or a report alone |
30: | **Owns** | The standard at `references/hvr-rules.md`, and the workflow that applies it |
31: | **Does not own** | The document-level audit. Structure, the Document Quality Index and the validators belong to `sk-create-quality-control` |
32: 
33: ---
34: 
35: ## 2. OVERVIEW
36: 
37: ### Why This Mode Exists
38: 
39: The Human Voice Rules have been in this repository for a long time, and hundreds of files
40: point at them. What was missing was anything that ran them.
41: 
42: The standard describes what to aim for. Every consumer was left to eyeball 120 banned
43: terms, 7 punctuation rules and a dozen structural patterns by reading, which is exactly
44: the task attention is worst at. The nearest thing to enforcement was one step inside the
45: document-quality audit that said "flag only issues that matter" and named no method.
46: 
47: So this mode is the method. It answers what may be touched, what a machine can settle,
48: what a reader has to settle, how the arithmetic works, and what proof the pass produces.
49: 
50: ### What It Does Not Do
51: 
52: It does not restate the standard. Every rule, term and penalty stays in the one file at
53: `references/hvr-rules.md`, which the scanner reads at run time. No document in this packet
54: carries a second copy, and no consumer elsewhere does either. The one thing worse than an
55: unenforced standard is two versions of it disagreeing.
56: 
57: It also does not own the document-level audit. Structure, the Document Quality Index and
58: the validators belong to `sk-create-quality-control`. That mode audits a file end to end
59: and calls this one for the voice finding it reports.
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ## 3. QUICK START
64: 
65: **Step 1: Scan before you read.**
66: 
67: ```bash
68: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-with-human-voice/scripts/hvr_scan.py <file>
69: ```
70: 
71: You get the hard blockers, the soft deductions, a count per term and a mechanical ceiling.
72: It takes under a second and settles the part of the standard a reader is worst at.
73: 
74: **Step 2: Decide what the scanner may not touch.** Quotations, code, generated files and
75: released changelog entries are out. `references/scope-and-exemptions.md` has the classes,
76: and getting this wrong is how a voice pass breaks a working code sample.
77: 
78: **Step 3: Read for what the scanner cannot see.** Three-item lists, triple headers, setup
79: language, synonym cycling, fragmented headers, hedging. The scanner prints this list on
80: every run so a clean mechanical result is never mistaken for a clean document.
81: 
82: **Step 4: After editing, scan again and report both numbers.** A rewrite that only reports
83: its final score has proved nothing.
84: 
85: ---
86: 
87: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
88: 
89: The scanner parses its term lists out of the standard on every run. Section 6 gives the
90: hard blocker words, section 7 the phrase blockers, section 8 the soft deductions and
91: section 3 the punctuation bans. Nothing is hardcoded, so editing the standard changes the
92: scan on the next invocation with no second file to update.
93: 
94: It masks what the standard does not govern before it looks: frontmatter, fenced blocks and
95: inline code spans, with the spans replaced by spaces so line and column numbers stay true.
96: `--include-code` turns that off when you actually want to scan a sample.
97: 
98: Findings are collapsed under the standard's own precedence rule. One occurrence costs one
99: penalty, the longest matching term wins, and a word listed as both an extended blocker and
100: context-dependent is charged once rather than twice.
101: 
102: ### Key Concept: It Over-Reports On Purpose
103: 
104: Scanning `sk-create-repo-rule/README.md`, a document written to this standard and reviewed
105: before it shipped, finds two hard blockers. Both are the word `harness`, used as a noun
106: meaning the AI runtime. That is the literal sense the standard permits, so the right
107: outcome is two recorded exemptions and no edit at all.
108: 
109: A scanner that tried to tell those apart would need to read for meaning, and one that
110: guessed would start hiding real findings. Over-reporting costs a reader a second per
111: candidate. Under-reporting ships the tell.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
116: 
117: ### When To Use This Mode
118: 
119: Reach for it when a draft reads as machine-written, when a document is about to ship and
120: wants a voice pass, when someone asks how prose scores without wanting edits, or when you
121: are about to write documentation and want the standard in force from the first sentence.
122: 
123: Skip it when the target needs a structural audit rather than a voice pass, when the
124: artifact does not exist yet, or when the text is something you are carrying rather than
125: writing.
126: 
127: ### Related Skills
128: 
129: | Skill | Relationship |
130: |---|---|
131: | `sk-create-quality-control` | Owns the file-level audit: structure, DQI and validators. Calls this mode for its voice step |
132: | `sk-create-readme` | Owns README structure. This mode passes over the prose those templates produce |
133: | `sk-create-repo-rule` | Owns repo-local rules. A rule about writing style would route here instead |
134: 
135: ---
136: 
137: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
138: 
139: | What you see | Why | Fix |
140: |---|---|---|
141: | A hard blocker on a word used literally | The scanner matches spelling, not sense. `harness` the noun, `landscape` in photography, `journey` when someone travelled | Record an exemption. Do not edit the sentence |
142: | Dozens of `do`, `get`, `make`, `take` findings | The standard's vague-verb list is real and very common | Fix the ones where a specific verb is clearly better. Density matters here, not the raw count |
143: | A negative score on a long reference | The 100-point scale assumes a piece, not a 900-line document | Report hard blockers and deductions per hundred lines, and say that is what you did |
144: | `exit 2` and a "parsed too thin" message | The standard's section headings changed and the parser no longer finds a list | Fix the parser. The scanner refuses to report a clean scan it never performed |
145: | A finding inside a code block | `--include-code` was passed, or the fence is malformed | Drop the flag, or repair the fence |
146: | Findings on `hvr-rules.md` itself | It lists every banned term, so it fails against itself | Do not score documents about the standard |
147: 
148: ---
149: 
150: ## 7. FAQ
151: 
152: **Q: Why does the standard sit in this packet rather than the hub's shared tier?**
153: 
154: A: Shared means every mode may reach it. Exactly one mode applies it, and one more reaches
155: it through a declared alias, so the shared placement bought a hop and no reuse. The move
156: repointed the live consumers, including the scanner, the hub router and the spec-kit
157: templates. Frozen spec documents and released changelog entries kept the old path, because
158: they record what was true when they were written.
159: 
160: **Q: Does a clean scan mean the document passes?**
161: 
162: A: No, and the scanner says so on every run. It covers the punctuation bans and the term
163: lists. Structure, rhythm, synonym cycling, significance inflation and whether the writing
164: has any personality all need a reader.
165: 
166: **Q: What happens when the standard and accuracy disagree?**
167: 
168: A: Accuracy wins and the exception gets recorded. A document that reads beautifully and
169: says something false has failed at the only thing that mattered.
170: 
171: **Q: Why does the scan run before the reading?**
172: 
173: A: Because it is cheap and complete over its own subset. A reader who starts with rhythm
174: spends their attention there while a hard blocker sits unfixed on line 8.
175: 
176: **Q: Can I scan something that is not markdown?**
177: 
178: A: Yes. Pass a path or pipe the text in on stdin. Frontmatter and fence masking simply
179: find nothing to mask.
180: 
181: ---
182: 
183: ## 8. VERIFICATION
184: 
185: | Check | How to run it | What a pass looks like |
186: |---|---|---|
187: | Dirty fixture | `python3 scripts/hvr_scan.py scripts/tests/fixtures/voice-dirty.md` | 6 hard blockers, exit 1, and nothing reported from the fenced block or the inline code span |

16: # create-with-human-voice
17: 
18: > Turn a draft that reads like a machine wrote it into one that does not, and show the numbers that prove the pass happened.
19: 
20: ---
21: 
22: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
23: 
24: | Aspect | What you get |
25: |---|---|
26: | **Use it for** | Applying the Human Voice Rules to prose, or scoring prose against them |
27: | **Invoke with** | `@markdown /create:with-human-voice`, which the command requires and hard-blocks without, or "make this sound human", or a direct read of `SKILL.md` |
28: | **Works on** | A file, a passage, a reply, or a draft you are part way through |
29: | **Produces** | An edited target plus a before and after report, or a report alone |
30: | **Owns** | The standard at `references/hvr-rules.md`, and the workflow that applies it |
31: | **Does not own** | The document-level audit. Structure, the Document Quality Index and the validators belong to `sk-create-quality-control` |
32: 
33: ---
34: 
35: ## 2. OVERVIEW
36: 
37: ### Why This Mode Exists
38: 
39: The Human Voice Rules have been in this repository for a long time, and hundreds of files
40: point at them. What was missing was anything that ran them.
41: 
42: The standard describes what to aim for. Every consumer was left to eyeball 120 banned
43: terms, 7 punctuation rules and a dozen structural patterns by reading, which is exactly
44: the task attention is worst at. The nearest thing to enforcement was one step inside the
45: document-quality audit that said "flag only issues that matter" and named no method.
46: 
47: So this mode is the method. It answers what may be touched, what a machine can settle,
48: what a reader has to settle, how the arithmetic works, and what proof the pass produces.
49: 
50: ### What It Does Not Do
51: 
52: It does not restate the standard. Every rule, term and penalty stays in the one file at
53: `references/hvr-rules.md`, which the scanner reads at run time. No document in this packet
54: carries a second copy, and no consumer elsewhere does either. The one thing worse than an
55: unenforced standard is two versions of it disagreeing.
56: 
57: It also does not own the document-level audit. Structure, the Document Quality Index and
58: the validators belong to `sk-create-quality-control`. That mode audits a file end to end
59: and calls this one for the voice finding it reports.
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ## 3. QUICK START
64: 
65: **Step 1: Scan before you read.**
66: 
67: ```bash
68: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-with-human-voice/scripts/hvr_scan.py <file>
69: ```
70: 
71: You get the hard blockers, the soft deductions, a count per term and a mechanical ceiling.
72: It takes under a second and settles the part of the standard a reader is worst at.
73: 
74: **Step 2: Decide what the scanner may not touch.** Quotations, code, generated files and
75: released changelog entries are out. `references/scope-and-exemptions.md` has the classes,
76: and getting this wrong is how a voice pass breaks a working code sample.
77: 
78: **Step 3: Read for what the scanner cannot see.** Three-item lists, triple headers, setup
79: language, synonym cycling, fragmented headers, hedging. The scanner prints this list on
80: every run so a clean mechanical result is never mistaken for a clean document.
81: 
82: **Step 4: After editing, scan again and report both numbers.** A rewrite that only reports
83: its final score has proved nothing.
84: 
85: ---
86: 
87: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
88: 
89: The scanner parses its term lists out of the standard on every run. Section 6 gives the
90: hard blocker words, section 7 the phrase blockers, section 8 the soft deductions and
91: section 3 the punctuation bans. Nothing is hardcoded, so editing the standard changes the
92: scan on the next invocation with no second file to update.
93: 
94: It masks what the standard does not govern before it looks: frontmatter, fenced blocks and
95: inline code spans, with the spans replaced by spaces so line and column numbers stay true.
96: `--include-code` turns that off when you actually want to scan a sample.
97: 
98: Findings are collapsed under the standard's own precedence rule. One occurrence costs one
99: penalty, the longest matching term wins, and a word listed as both an extended blocker and
100: context-dependent is charged once rather than twice.
101: 
102: ### Key Concept: It Over-Reports On Purpose
103: 
104: Scanning `sk-create-repo-rule/README.md`, a document written to this standard and reviewed
105: before it shipped, finds two hard blockers. Both are the word `harness`, used as a noun
106: meaning the AI runtime. That is the literal sense the standard permits, so the right
107: outcome is two recorded exemptions and no edit at all.
108: 
109: A scanner that tried to tell those apart would need to read for meaning, and one that
110: guessed would start hiding real findings. Over-reporting costs a reader a second per
111: candidate. Under-reporting ships the tell.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
116: 
117: ### When To Use This Mode
118: 
119: Reach for it when a draft reads as machine-written, when a document is about to ship and
120: wants a voice pass, when someone asks how prose scores without wanting edits, or when you
121: are about to write documentation and want the standard in force from the first sentence.
122: 
123: Skip it when the target needs a structural audit rather than a voice pass, when the
124: artifact does not exist yet, or when the text is something you are carrying rather than
125: writing.
126: 
127: ### Related Skills
128: 
129: | Skill | Relationship |
130: |---|---|
131: | `sk-create-quality-control` | Owns the file-level audit: structure, DQI and validators. Calls this mode for its voice step |
132: | `sk-create-readme` | Owns README structure. This mode passes over the prose those templates produce |
133: | `sk-create-repo-rule` | Owns repo-local rules. A rule about writing style would route here instead |
134: 
135: ---
136: 
137: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
138: 
139: | What you see | Why | Fix |
140: |---|---|---|
141: | A hard blocker on a word used literally | The scanner matches spelling, not sense. `harness` the noun, `landscape` in photography, `journey` when someone travelled | Record an exemption. Do not edit the sentence |
142: | Dozens of `do`, `get`, `make`, `take` findings | The standard's vague-verb list is real and very common | Fix the ones where a specific verb is clearly better. Density matters here, not the raw count |
143: | A negative score on a long reference | The 100-point scale assumes a piece, not a 900-line document | Report hard blockers and deductions per hundred lines, and say that is what you did |
144: | `exit 2` and a "parsed too thin" message | The standard's section headings changed and the parser no longer finds a list | Fix the parser. The scanner refuses to report a clean scan it never performed |
145: | A finding inside a code block | `--include-code` was passed, or the fence is malformed | Drop the flag, or repair the fence |
146: | Findings on `hvr-rules.md` itself | It lists every banned term, so it fails against itself | Do not score documents about the standard |
147: 
148: ---
149: 
150: ## 7. FAQ
151: 
152: **Q: Why does the standard sit in this packet rather than the hub's shared tier?**
153: 
154: A: Shared means every mode may reach it. Exactly one mode applies it, and one more reaches
155: it through a declared alias, so the shared placement bought a hop and no reuse. The move
156: repointed the live consumers, including the scanner, the hub router and the spec-kit
157: templates. Frozen spec documents and released changelog entries kept the old path, because
158: they record what was true when they were written.
159: 
160: **Q: Does a clean scan mean the document passes?**
161: 
162: A: No, and the scanner says so on every run. It covers the punctuation bans and the term
163: lists. Structure, rhythm, synonym cycling, significance inflation and whether the writing
164: has any personality all need a reader.
165: 
166: **Q: What happens when the standard and accuracy disagree?**
167: 
168: A: Accuracy wins and the exception gets recorded. A document that reads beautifully and
169: says something false has failed at the only thing that mattered.
170: 
171: **Q: Why does the scan run before the reading?**
172: 
173: A: Because it is cheap and complete over its own subset. A reader who starts with rhythm
174: spends their attention there while a hard blocker sits unfixed on line 8.
175: 
176: **Q: Can I scan something that is not markdown?**
177: 
178: A: Yes. Pass a path or pipe the text in on stdin. Frontmatter and fence masking simply
179: find nothing to mask.
180: 
181: ---
182: 
183: ## 8. VERIFICATION
184: 
185: | Check | How to run it | What a pass looks like |
186: |---|---|---|
187: | Dirty fixture | `python3 scripts/hvr_scan.py scripts/tests/fixtures/voice-dirty.md` | 6 hard blockers, exit 1, and nothing reported from the fenced block or the inline code span |

191: | Packet contract | `python3 ../sk-create-skill/scripts/package_skill.py . --check --strict` | `Result: PASS` |

13: # Voice Report Template
14: 
15: The fixed shape of a voice-pass result, filled in once per run.
16: 
17: ## 1. OVERVIEW
18: 
19: ### Purpose
20: 
21: A voice pass is only as good as its record. This blank forces the pass to state what it
22: was allowed to touch, what it measured before and after, what it declined, and what a
23: reader still owns.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Copy the block in section 2 and fill every row. A row with nothing to report says `None`,
28: which is a finding in itself. A row you delete reads as a step you skipped. Drop the two
29: after-columns on a `score` run, where nothing was edited.
30: 
31: ---
32: 
33: ## 2. TEMPLATE
34: 
35: ```markdown
36: **Target**
37: - Path or span: `<file, or a description of the passage>`
38: - Operation: `<apply|score>`
39: - Length basis: `<absolute score|hard blockers + density>`
40: 
41: **Scope**
42: - In scope: `<what the pass was allowed to touch>`
43: - Exempt: `<span>`, `<class from scope-and-exemptions.md section 3>`, `<why>`
44: - Exempt: `<span>`, `<class>`, `<why>`
45: 
46: **Mechanical scan**
47: | | Before | After |
48: |---|---|---|
49: | Hard blockers | `<n>` | `<n>` |
50: | Deductions | `-<n>` | `-<n>` |
51: | Ceiling | `<n>/100` | `<n>/100` |
52: - Source: `scripts/hvr_scan.py` against `references/hvr-rules.md`
53: 
54: **Judgment findings**
55: - `<structural, sentence-level, content or voice finding>`: `<fixed|left, with reason>`
56: 
57: **Accepted exceptions**
58: - `<term or construction kept>`: `<what would have changed if it were removed>`
59: 
60: **Verdict**
61: - Band: `<publish|revise|rewrite>`
62: - Remaining: `<what a reader still has to decide, or None>`
63: ```
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 3. WHY EACH ROW IS THERE
68: 
69: **Length basis** stops an absolute score being quoted for a document too long to carry
70: one. Say which measure you used before you quote a number from it.
71: 
72: **Exempt** rows are the record that a finding was seen and declined. Without them the next
73: pass re-flags the same span, and the pass after that re-flags it again.
74: 
75: **Before and after** columns are the proof the edit landed. One number alone proves
76: nothing, and a rewrite that scores worse than the draft is a result worth reporting rather
77: than hiding.
78: 
79: **Accepted exceptions** is where accuracy beating the standard gets written down. A kept
80: banned word with a stated reason is a decision. The same word with no note is a miss.
81: 
82: **Remaining** is honest handoff. Nothing in the judgment pass is machine-settled, so
83: handing back a list of what a reader still owns costs a line and saves a re-read.
84:

18: 
19: ### Purpose
20: 
21: A voice pass is only as good as its record. This blank forces the pass to state what it
22: was allowed to touch, what it measured before and after, what it declined, and what a
23: reader still owns.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Copy the block in section 2 and fill every row. A row with nothing to report says `None`,
28: which is a finding in itself. A row you delete reads as a step you skipped. Drop the two
29: after-columns on a `score` run, where nothing was edited.
30: 
31: ---
32: 
33: ## 2. TEMPLATE
34: 
35: ```markdown
36: **Target**
37: - Path or span: `<file, or a description of the passage>`
38: - Operation: `<apply|score>`
39: - Length basis: `<absolute score|hard blockers + density>`
40: 
41: **Scope**
42: - In scope: `<what the pass was allowed to touch>`
43: - Exempt: `<span>`, `<class from scope-and-exemptions.md section 3>`, `<why>`
44: - Exempt: `<span>`, `<class>`, `<why>`
45: 
46: **Mechanical scan**
47: | | Before | After |
48: |---|---|---|
49: | Hard blockers | `<n>` | `<n>` |
50: | Deductions | `-<n>` | `-<n>` |
51: | Ceiling | `<n>/100` | `<n>/100` |
52: - Source: `scripts/hvr_scan.py` against `references/hvr-rules.md`
53: 
54: **Judgment findings**
55: - `<structural, sentence-level, content or voice finding>`: `<fixed|left, with reason>`
56: 
57: **Accepted exceptions**
58: - `<term or construction kept>`: `<what would have changed if it were removed>`
59: 
60: **Verdict**
61: - Band: `<publish|revise|rewrite>`
62: - Remaining: `<what a reader still has to decide, or None>`
63: ```

68: 
69: **Length basis** stops an absolute score being quoted for a document too long to carry
70: one. Say which measure you used before you quote a number from it.
71: 
72: **Exempt** rows are the record that a finding was seen and declined. Without them the next
73: pass re-flags the same span, and the pass after that re-flags it again.
74: 
75: **Before and after** columns are the proof the edit landed. One number alone proves
76: nothing, and a rewrite that scores worse than the draft is a result worth reporting rather
77: than hiding.
78: 
79: **Accepted exceptions** is where accuracy beating the standard gets written down. A kept
80: banned word with a stated reason is a decision. The same word with no note is a miss.
81: 
82: **Remaining** is honest handoff. Nothing in the judgment pass is machine-settled, so
83: handing back a list of what a reader still owns costs a line and saves a re-read.

15: # Human Voice Rules (HVR) - Writing Standards Reference
16: 
17: Linguistic standards for all documentation output. These rules eliminate AI-detectable patterns and ensure every piece of writing reads as if a knowledgeable human wrote it.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: AI-generated text carries tells: em dashes everywhere, three-item lists, hedging language, the same 20 overused words. Readers spot these patterns and trust drops. HVR defines what to aim for and what to avoid.
26: 
27: ### Usage
28: 
29: Apply to all AI-generated documentation: READMEs, implementation summaries, decision records, install guides and spec folder docs.
30: 
31: A reply loads this file, and a document also loads the publish supplement, `hvr-publish-supplement.md`.
32: 
33: - Read the voice directives (Section 2) to understand the target voice
34: - Use word lists (Sections 6-8) as reference during writing
35: - Run the pre-publish checklist in `hvr-publish-supplement.md` before finalizing
36: 
37: ---
38: 
39: ## 2. VOICE DIRECTIVES
40: 
41: ```yaml
42: voice_directives:
43:   active_voice:
44:     directive: "Use active voice. Subject before verb."
45:     wrong: "The meeting was cancelled by management."
46:     right: "Management cancelled the meeting."
47: 
48:   direct_address:
49:     directive: "Address the reader with 'you' and 'your'."
50:     wrong: "Users will find that the platform saves time."
51:     right: "You'll find the platform saves time."
52: 
53:   conciseness:
54:     directive: "Be direct. Cut fluff. Say it in fewer words."
55:     wrong: "It is important to note that the deadline is on Friday."
56:     right: "The deadline is Friday."
57: 
58:   simple_language:
59:     directive: "Use common words. If a simpler word exists, use it."
60:     wrong: "We need to facilitate the optimisation of our workflow processes."
61:     right: "We need to fix how we work."
62: 
63:   clarity:
64:     directive: "One idea per sentence when possible."
65:     wrong: "The platform, which was built last year by our engineering team who worked remotely, handles data processing and also does analytics while maintaining uptime."
66:     right: "The platform handles data processing and analytics. Our engineering team built it last year."
67: 
68:   conversational_tone:
69:     directive: "Write naturally. Read it aloud. If it sounds stiff, rewrite it."
70:     wrong: "One must consider the implications of such a decision."
71:     right: "Think about what this decision means."
72: 
73:   authenticity:
74:     directive: "Be honest. If something has problems, say so. No marketing spin."
75:     wrong: "Our revolutionary solution transforms every aspect of your workflow."
76:     right: "Our tool automates three manual steps in your invoicing process."
77: 
78:   practical_focus:
79:     directive: "Focus on actionable information. Back claims with data or examples."
80:     wrong: "Many companies have seen great success."
81:     right: "Acme Corp cut onboarding time from 3 weeks to 4 days."
82: 
83:   sentence_rhythm:
84:     directive: "Vary sentence lengths. Mix short (under 8 words) with medium (8-15) and long (15-25)."
85: 
86:   certainty:
87:     directive: "Prefer certainty when facts support it. Hedging weakens claims."
88:     wrong: "This approach might improve results."
89:     right: "This approach improves results."
90:     note: "Hedge only when genuine uncertainty exists."
91: ```
92: 
93: The directives above state the target. Two tests and one exemplar decide whether a draft reaches it.
94: 
95: **Borrowability.** If any writer could have produced the sentence, it carries no sourcing. Rewrite it from what you actually observed. The failure it prevents: prose anyone could have written.
96: 
97: **Plain word.** When two words hold the same precision, keep the one with the concrete root. "Start" beats "commence". The failure it prevents: Latinate abstraction where a plain word holds the same precision.
98: 
99: **The exemplar.** One paragraph, written as this section prescribes:
100: 
101: ```
102: We ran the migration at 2am. It finished in 9 minutes, not the 40 the old path needed. Two services stalled. The retry loop caught both. We migrated the remaining services the next morning.
103: ```
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ## 3. PUNCTUATION STANDARDS
108: 
109: | Rule | Symbol | Action | Replace With |
110: |------|--------|--------|--------------|
111: | **Em Dash Ban** | — | NEVER use | Comma, full stop or colon |
112: | **Semicolon Ban** | ; | NEVER use | Two sentences, or a conjunction |
113: | **Oxford Comma Ban** | , and | NEVER use | Drop the comma before "and"/"or" |
114: | **Asterisk Emphasis** | * | NEVER in output | Natural word weight (OK in Markdown source) |
115: | **Ellipsis** | ... | Max 1 per piece | Trailing thought only, never dramatic pauses |
116: | **Quotation Marks** | " " | Straight quotes only | Never curly quotes (" ") |
117: | **Emoji** | 🎯 | Max 1 per piece | Must add clarity or tone, not decoration |
118: 
119: **Examples:**
120: ```
121: Em dash:    WRONG: "The platform — built for speed — handles millions."
122:             RIGHT: "The platform, built for speed, handles millions."
123: 
124: Semicolon:  WRONG: "The data was clear; the market was shifting."
125:             RIGHT: "The data was clear. The market was shifting."
126: 
127: Oxford:     WRONG: "revenue, retention, and churn"
128:             RIGHT: "revenue, retention and churn"
129: ```
130: 
131: ---
132: 
133: ## 4. AI STRUCTURAL PATTERNS TO AVOID
134: 
135: ### "Not Just X, But Also Y" Ban
136: 
137: Never use this construction or variants: "not only X but Y", "it's not X, it's Y", "more than just X". Lead with the stronger point or use "and".
138: 
139: ```
140: WRONG: "Not just a tool, but a complete platform."
141: RIGHT: "A complete platform."
142: ```
143: 
144: ### Tables In A Reply
145: 
146: Scoped to a conversational reply, never to a document. A document is returned to and
147: scanned, so a table earns its place there. A reply is read once, and a grid makes the
148: reader parse rows and columns to reach one fact that a sentence would have handed them.
149: 
150: Put one or two facts in a sentence. Put parallel items in a bulleted list. Reserve the
151: table for a file someone comes back to.
152: 
153: ```
154: WRONG (in a reply):
155: | File | What changed |
156: |------|--------------|
157: | a.md | trimmed      |
158: 
159: RIGHT (in a reply):
160: Trimmed `a.md`.
161: ```
162: 
163: ### Literal Over Figurative
164: 
165: In a reply, replace an idiom the reader must decode with the plain statement. The failure it prevents: a reader decoding instead of reading.
166: 
167: ```
168: WRONG: "We should circle back on the pricing next week."
169: RIGHT: "I will send you the pricing next week."
170: ```
171: 
172: ### Three-Item Enumeration Fix
173: 
174: AI defaults to exactly three items. Use 2, 4 or 5 instead. If you naturally have 3, cut one or add a fourth.
175: 
176: ### Triple-Header Pattern Fix
177: 
178: AI tends to use exactly three H3 subsections under each H2 section. Vary the count. Use 2, 4 or 5 subsections based on actual content needs. If you genuinely have three subsections, verify each one carries its weight.
179: 
180: ### Setup Language Removal
181: 
182: Cut these filler phrases that signal what's coming instead of stating it:
183: 
184: - "In conclusion" / "In summary"
185: - "It's worth noting" / "It's important to note"
186: - "Let's explore" / "Let's dive in" / "Let's take a look"
187: - "When it comes to" / "In the world of"
188: - "In today's [X]" / "At its core"
189: - "At the end of the day" / "Without further ado"
190: - "As we all know" / "It goes without saying"
191: - "First and foremost" / "Last but not least"
192: - "With that in mind" / "On that note" / "That said"
193: - "In simple terms" / "Simply put" / "Put simply"
194: 
195: ### Analogy Overuse Fix
196: 
197: Analogies help readers grasp technical concepts. Overusing them is an AI tell.
198: 
199: | Rule | Limit | Example |
200: |------|-------|---------|
201: | **One analogy per concept** | 1 max | Do not stack "like a librarian" and "like a filing cabinet" for the same feature |
202: | **"Think of it as/like"** | 2 per document max | Third occurrence signals AI pattern |
203: | **Placement** | After the technical statement | State the fact first, then the analogy. Never lead with the analogy. |
204: | **Drop when unnecessary** | If plain language is clear | "The script validates inputs" needs no analogy |
205: 
206: ### Nominalization And Stacked Compression
207: 
208: Turn the noun back into its verb, then cut the metaphor. The failure it prevents: abstract nouns hiding actions, metaphor piled on nominalization.
209: 
210: ```
211: WRONG: "The implementation of the optimization delivers a bridge between the two systems."
212: RIGHT: "The optimization connects the two systems."
213: ```
214: 
215: ### Banned Metaphors
216: 
217: Replace with direct language:
218: 
219: | Banned | Use Instead |
220: |--------|-------------|
221: | "bridge the gap" | "connect" |
222: | "tip of the iceberg" | "one example" |
223: | "pave the way" | "enable" |
224: | "game-changer" | state the specific change |
225: | "move the needle" | state the specific metric |
226: | "low-hanging fruit" | "quick win" |
227: | "deep dive" | "detailed look" |
228: | "at the heart of" | "central to" |
229: | "a world where" | remove or rephrase |
230: | "raise the bar" | "improve" |
231: | "double-edged sword" | "trade-off" |
232: | "level the playing field" | "equalise access" |
233: | "perfect storm" | state the specific factors |
234: | "elephant in the room" | state the issue directly |
235: | "the bottom line" | state the conclusion |
236: | "food for thought" | remove entirely |
237: | "breath of fresh air" | state what's different |
238: | "light at the end of the tunnel" | state the positive outcome |
239: 
240: ### Generalisation Fixes
241: 
242: Replace vague claims with specifics:
243: 
244: | Vague | Fix |
245: |-------|-----|
246: | "Many companies" | Name the company or give a number |
247: | "Studies show" | Name the study and year |
248: | "Experts agree" | Name the expert |
249: | "In recent years" | Give the specific year or date |
250: | "A growing number of" | State the number or percentage |
251: | "Research suggests" | Name the institution and year |
252: | "Industry leaders" | Name the companies or people |
253: | "Some people" | State who, or give a number |
254: 
255: ### Unnecessary Modifiers
256: 
257: Cut these words. They add no meaning: very, really, truly, absolutely, incredibly, extremely, quite, rather, somewhat, fairly, just, actually, basically, literally, simply, obviously, clearly, certainly, definitely, undoubtedly, essentially.
258: 
259: ### Copula Avoidance Ban
260: 
261: When "is" or "are" works, use it. Do not substitute elaborate constructions.
262: 
263: | Banned Substitute | Use Instead |
264: |-------------------|-------------|
265: | "serves as" | "is" |
266: | "stands as" | "is" |
267: | "functions as" | "is" |
268: | "acts as" | "is" (when not literal acting) |
269: | "boasts" | "has" |
270: | "features" | "has" or "includes" |
271: | "offers" | "has" or "provides" (when describing attributes) |
272: 
273: Acceptable when they add genuine meaning (e.g., "The firewall acts as a barrier").
274: 
275: ### Synonym Cycling Fix
276: 
277: When referring to the same thing, use the same word. AI cycles through synonyms because of repetition penalties. If you write "the server" in one sentence, do not switch to "the system" and then "the platform" in the next two. Natural variation (e.g., a name and "she") is fine. The signal is 3+ different words for the same entity in one piece.
278: 
279: ### False Ranges
280: 
281: Remove "from X to Y" constructions where the endpoints are not on a meaningful scale.
282: 
283: ```
284: WRONG: "From startups to enterprises, everyone benefits."
285: RIGHT: "Startups and enterprises both benefit."
286: 
287: OK: "Temperatures range from -10C to 40C." (genuine measurable range)
288: ```
289: 
290: ### Generic Positive Conclusions
291: 
292: End with specifics, not sentiments. Never use these closers:
293: 
294: - "The future looks bright"
295: - "Exciting times lie ahead"
296: - "This represents a major step forward"
297: - "The possibilities are endless"
298: - "We look forward to what's next"
299: - "This is just the beginning"
300: - "The best is yet to come"
301: 
302: ### Fragmented Headers
303: 
304: Remove generic sentences that restate the heading. Jump straight to substance.
305: 
306: ```
307: WRONG:
308: ### Error Handling
309: Error handling is an important part of any application.
310: [actual content follows]
311: 
312: RIGHT:
313: ### Error Handling
314: The API returns structured JSON errors with HTTP status codes and machine-readable error types.
315: ```
316: 
317: ### Significance Inflation
318: 
319: State what happened without editorialising its importance. If something genuinely is a turning point, provide evidence instead of declaring it.
320: 
321: Banned phrases:
322: - "marks a pivotal moment in"
323: - "setting the stage for"
324: - "indelible mark"
325: - "is a testament to"
326: - "underscores the importance of"
327: - "reflects broader trends in"
328: - "represents a shift in"
329: - "shaping the future of"
330: 
331: ### Output Warnings
332: 
333: Never include meta-commentary about the writing process. No disclaimers about tone. No references to these rules in output. No "I've kept this concise" or "I avoided jargon." No knowledge-cutoff disclaimers ("as of my last update", "based on available information"). No training-data hedging ("Up to my last training update").
334: 
335: ---
336: 
337: ## 5. VOICE PERSONALITY
338: 
339: This section binds writing you own. A projection or rewrite that carries someone else's message skips it, because a reaction the original never held is a fidelity defect.
340: 
341: Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing that follows every rule can still read as AI-generated. Clean writing needs personality.
342: 
343: ### Have Opinions
344: 
345: React to facts. Do not just report them neutrally.
346: 
347: ```
348: FLAT:   "The results were mixed."
349: VOICED: "The results surprised us. Half the metrics improved while the others dropped."
350: ```
351: 
352: ### Acknowledge Complexity
353: 
354: Express mixed feelings. Real people do not sort everything into neat categories. When something has trade-offs, say so instead of presenting a clean conclusion.
355: 
356: ### Controlled Imperfection
357: 
358: Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Allow occasional tangents and asides when they add authenticity. This does not override conciseness or clarity. It means choosing natural flow over mechanical symmetry.
359: 
360: ### Emotional Specificity
361: 
362: Name specific feelings and images, not abstract labels.
363: 
364: ```
365: ABSTRACT: "The results were disappointing."
366: SPECIFIC: "We expected at least a 10% lift. We got 2%."
367: ```
368: 
369: ---
370: 
371: ## 6. HARD BLOCKER WORDS
372: 
373: Never use these. Each occurrence is automatic failure.
374: 
375: **Core blockers:**
376: `delve`, `embark`, `realm`, `tapestry`, `illuminate`, `unveil`, `elucidate`, `abyss`, `revolutionise`, `game-changer`, `groundbreaking`, `cutting-edge`, `ever-evolving`, `shed light`, `dive deep`
377: 
378: **Extended blockers:**
379: `leverage` (use "use"), `foster` (use "support"), `nurture` (use "develop"), `resonate` (use "connect with"), `empower` (use "enable"), `disrupt` (use "change"), `curate` (use "select"), `harness` (use "use"), `elevate` (use "improve"), `robust` (use "strong"), `seamless` (use "smooth"), `holistic` (use "complete"), `synergy` (use "combined effect"), `unpack` (use "explain"), `landscape` (as industry noun), `ecosystem` (as metaphor), `journey` (as process metaphor), `paradigm` (use "model"), `enlightening` (use "helpful"), `esteemed` (use "respected"), `remarkable` (use "notable"), `skyrocket/skyrocketing` (use "increase"), `utilize/utilizing` (use "use/using")
380: 
381: **Context-dependent** (-5 when metaphorical, OK when literal):
382: `navigating` (blocked: challenges | OK: website), `landscape` (blocked: competitive | OK: photography), `unlock` (blocked: potential | OK: door), `ecosystem` (blocked: startup | OK: biological), `journey` (blocked: customer | OK: actual travel)
383: 
384: ---
385: 
386: ## 7. PHRASE HARD BLOCKERS
387: 
388: Never use any of these:
389: 
390: - "It's important to" / "It's worth noting"
391: - "It goes without saying" / "At the end of the day"
392: - "Moving forward" / "In today's world"
393: - "In today's digital landscape"
394: - "When it comes to" / "Dive into"
395: - "I'd love to" / "Navigating the [X]"
396: - "That being said" / "Having said that"
397: - "Let me be clear" / "The reality is"
398: - "Here's the thing" / "In a world where"
399: - "You're not alone"
400: - "The real question is" / "The truth is"
401: - "Here's what you need to know" / "What most people don't realise is"
402: 
403: ---
404: 
405: ## 8. SOFT DEDUCTIONS
406: 
407: ### -2 Points Each
408: 
409: | Word | Note |
410: |------|------|
411: | craft/crafting | As verb for "create". OK as noun (craft beer). |
412: | pivotal | Use "important" or "key" |
413: | intricate | Use "complex" or "detailed" |
414: | testament | Use "proof" or "evidence" |
415: | disruptive | Use "new" or describe the change |
416: | transformative | Use "significant" or describe the effect |
417: | innovative | Use "new" or describe what's different |
418: | impactful | Use "effective" or "significant" |
419: | scalable | When used as buzzword. OK in genuine technical contexts. |
420: | actionable | When used as buzzword. OK in genuine instruction contexts. |
421: | strategic | When used as filler adjective. OK in genuine strategy contexts. |
422: | remains to be seen | Use "we don't know yet" |
423: | glimpse into | Use "look at" or "overview of" |
424: | you're not alone | AI comfort phrase. State the specific commonality. |
425: | discover | When hype. OK in factual discovery contexts. |
426: 
427: ### -1 Point Each
428: 
429: **Hedging:** "I think", "I believe", "perhaps", "maybe", "might", "could potentially", "probably"
430: 
431: **Filler:** "actually", "basically", "essentially", "literally", "honestly", "frankly"
432: 
433: **Transitions** (penalty on 3rd+ use): "however", "furthermore", "moreover", "additionally", "consequently"
434: 
435: **Weak adjectives:** "nice", "good", "great", "amazing", "awesome", "incredible", "fantastic", "wonderful", "stark" (use "clear"), "powerful" (when filler)
436: 
437: **Vague verbs:** "get" (use specific: obtain, receive), "do" (use: complete, execute), "make" (use: build, create), "put" (use: place, position), "take" (use: accept, adopt, require), "opened up" (use: created, enabled)
438: 
439: **AI phrases:** "I'd be happy to", "Great question", "That's a great point", "I appreciate you sharing", "Let me help you with that", "imagine" (as setup), "exciting" (as AI enthusiasm)
440: 
441: **Buzzwords:** "synergise", "operationalise", "incentivise", "circle back", "move the needle", "low-hanging fruit", "boost" (as hype filler), "inquiries" (use "questions")
442: 
443: ### Context Flags (not penalised, but check)
444: 
445: - **"it"** - Does it have a clear antecedent? Replace with specific noun if ambiguous.
446: - **"this"** - Always follow with a noun: "This decline" not just "This".
447: - **"things"/"stuff"** - Replace with specific noun.
448: - **"solution"** - Overused in B2B. Say what it is: platform, tool, service.
449: - **"excited"** - AI-typical enthusiasm. State the specific reason for interest instead.

15: # Human Voice Rules (HVR) - Writing Standards Reference
16:

22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: AI-generated text carries tells: em dashes everywhere, three-item lists, hedging language, the same 20 overused words. Readers spot these patterns and trust drops. HVR defines what to aim for and what to avoid.

29: Apply to all AI-generated documentation: READMEs, implementation summaries, decision records, install guides and spec folder docs.

42: voice_directives:
43:   active_voice:
44:     directive: "Use active voice. Subject before verb."
45:     wrong: "The meeting was cancelled by management."
46:     right: "Management cancelled the meeting."
47: 
48:   direct_address:
49:     directive: "Address the reader with 'you' and 'your'."
50:     wrong: "Users will find that the platform saves time."
51:     right: "You'll find the platform saves time."
52: 
53:   conciseness:

61:     right: "We need to fix how we work."

63:   clarity:

65:     wrong: "The platform, which was built last year by our engineering team who worked remotely, handles data processing and also does analytics while maintaining uptime."
66:     right: "The platform handles data processing and analytics. Our engineering team built it last year."
67: 
68:   conversational_tone:
69:     directive: "Write naturally. Read it aloud. If it sounds stiff, rewrite it."
70:     wrong: "One must consider the implications of such a decision."
71:     right: "Think about what this decision means."
72:

85: 
86:   certainty:

88:     wrong: "This approach might improve results."
89:     right: "This approach improves results."
90:     note: "Hedge only when genuine uncertainty exists."
91: ```
